claims.text:
"Isengrim" is of Anglo-Saxon origin and comes from isen meaning "iron" and grim meaning "fierce".
It is likely Isengrim is named after an earlier Isengrim, but it is notable that "Isengrim" is the name of a wolf who appears in many medieval epics, including the story of Reynard the Fox which originated in French folklore.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Nomenclature of The Lord of the Rings" in Wayne G. Hammond and Christina Scull (eds), The Lord of the Rings: A Reader's Companion, p. 760

claims.text: The eldest son of the Old Took, Isengrim's rule was noticeably short. Due to his father's longevity, he was already near his nineties when he became Thain, and ruled for ten years before his death. As he had no children of his own, his brother Isumbras became the new Thain.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Took of Great Smials"
